summary.text: The Copenhagen interpretation is a family of views on what quantum mechanics means, growing out of the work of Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and others.
Versions share the ideas that nature is intrinsically indeterministic, that the Born rule gives probabilities, and that complementary properties cannot all be observed together.
There is no single official statement of it, since Bohr and Heisenberg never fully agreed, yet it remains one of the most commonly taught interpretations.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: The city where Bohr and Heisenberg worked

facts.label: Born rule
facts.value: The wave function yields probabilities for measurement outcomes

facts.label: Complementarity
facts.value: Some properties cannot be jointly defined at the same time

facts.label: Mermin's slogan
facts.value: "Shut up and calculate!" sums up Copenhagen-type views

items.prompt: A student asks where the one authoritative text of the Copenhagen interpretation can be found. What is the honest answer?

options.label: In one definitive paper by Bohr
In a joint statement they all signed
In a textbook by Max Born
None exists, and its founders disagree

items.explain: There is no definitive historical statement, and the writings of Bohr and Heisenberg contradict each other on several important issues.

items.prompt: In this view, what does the wave function of a system give you?

options.label: Probabilities for the outcomes of measurements
A guaranteed single outcome for each test
A movie of the exact path each particle takes
A list of hidden causes that fix results

items.explain: The Born rule says the wave function yields probabilities for measurement outcomes, and quantum mechanics is intrinsically indeterministic.

items.prompt: You set up an experiment to learn exactly where an electron is. Complementarity says what about the experiment you would need to learn its momentum instead?

options.label: The same arrangement gives both at once
It would need a different, mutually exclusive arrangement
The electron has no momentum
Nothing can be learned about it ever

items.explain: Observables belonging to mutually exclusive laboratory arrangements cannot be predicted together, yet considering several such experiments is needed to characterize a system.

items.prompt: Which describes how Copenhagen-type views treat the readings of a measuring device?

options.label: They are described by superposition equations only
They are hidden until the experiment ends
They are essentially classical, described in ordinary language
They are impossible to describe in words

items.explain: Results from measuring devices are essentially classical and should be described in ordinary language, as Bohr emphasized and Heisenberg accepted.

items.prompt: Why do some physicists object to the interpretation?

options.label: What counts as a measuring device is unclear
It is never taught in any university
Its probabilities fail in every experiment
It was only invented last year

items.explain: Objections include the abrupt, random nature of measurement, the difficulty of defining a measuring device, and the reliance on classical physics.

items.prompt: By the early 1920s, physicists were patching classical physics with approximations. What showed that approach was failing?

options.label: It worked perfectly for every atom
Heisenberg had not yet been born
The patches were never tried on hydrogen
One model could not go from hydrogen to helium

items.explain: From 1922 to 1925 the heuristic method met growing difficulties; for example the Bohr–Sommerfeld model could not go from hydrogen to helium.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Copenhagen interpretation is a family of ideas about what quantum mechanics really means, rooted in work by Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and others. Quantum mechanics does not sit easily with everyday language and experience, and even the people who built it often found it strange. The Copenhagen ideas offer one way to think about how the theory's mathematics connects to the physical world.

paragraphs.heading: The core ideas
paragraphs.text: Most versions share a few features. Quantum mechanics is taken to be indeterministic at its root, and it gives probabilities worked out with the Born rule, which turns a system's wave function into odds for each measurement result. Then there is complementarity: some pairs of properties of an object cannot all be observed or measured at once. Measuring an object is also irreversible, and nothing can be called true of it except what its measurement shows.

paragraphs.heading: The lab set-up matters
paragraphs.text: To talk about a particular property of a system, you have to picture that system inside a specific laboratory arrangement. Quantities tied to arrangements that exclude one another cannot be predicted together. Yet you still need several such experiments to describe the system fully. The readings that measuring devices give are basically classical and should be put in ordinary language, a point Bohr pressed hard and Heisenberg accepted.

paragraphs.heading: Born in the 1920s
paragraphs.text: The ideas took shape between 1925 and 1927. In 1925 Heisenberg described electrons using only quantities that could be observed, which for him meant the frequencies of light that atoms absorb and emit. Max Born saw that in this theory, position and momentum become matrices: mathematical objects that multiply like numbers, except that the order of multiplying changes the answer. When Erwin Schrödinger wrote an equation treating the electron as a wave, Born found that its wave function worked best as a tool for calculating probabilities.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: The name points to Copenhagen, the city where Bohr and Heisenberg worked. The label itself seems to have come from Heisenberg around 1955, while he was attacking rival interpretations such as David Bohm's. Before his book went on sale, Heisenberg privately regretted the term, because it implied that other interpretations existed, and he judged those to be nonsense. In 1960 Léon Rosenfeld, a close collaborator of Bohr, called it an ambiguous expression and proposed dropping it, but the name spread widely anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Many versions, still taught
paragraphs.text: There is no single official statement of the view. Bohr and Heisenberg wrote things that clash on several key issues, and Bohr kept his distance from what he saw as Heisenberg's more subjective reading. Asher Peres noted that different authors present very different, even opposite, views under the same name, and David Mermin spoke of its many flavors. Critics have objected to the sudden, random nature of measurement and to the trouble of saying what counts as a measuring device. Even so, it remains one of the most commonly taught interpretations.
